title: Competing Fault Histories in Lattice-Surgery Decoding
abstract: Different physical faults can produce the same detector record while carrying opposite logical labels. We investigate the consequence of this ambiguity for a lattice surgery parity measurement. In a distance-three merge--split circuit, single-gate faults compete with reset/readout pairs on three complete syndromes. Full-syndrome probabilities give a simultaneous 95\% lower confidence bound of $16.64$ parts per million on the cost of retaining the selected single-fault decisions at one noise point. Changing those decisions is harmful at low noise and beneficial at higher noise. To test the physical explanation, we attenuate eight implicated channels and compare the change in override effect with a matched non-target suppression. The two interventions change the decoder effect differently, resolving a contribution associated with those locations. Likelihood predictions fixed before sampling then select useful decisions under mixed Pauli noise and after extending preparation and recovery. The latter test gives a reduction of $13.20$ parts per million, with simultaneous 95\% bounds $[5.55,20.84]$. The mechanism is limited in scope: the revised decisions give up certain single-fault corrections, and under the same witness-selection rule no candidate is identified in the fully expanded distance-five circuit. These results connect a finite-noise decoding trade-off to specific physical channels and test how far that explanation can be used to predict logical-parity performance.
summary: This work analyzes the ambiguity in lattice-surgery decoding where multiple physical fault paths can yield the same measurement outcome but imply opposite logical states. By quantifying the performance trade-offs using full-syndrome probabilities and testing targeted channel suppressions, the authors map the limits of current decoding assumptions. The results provide a detailed, quantitative understanding of how noise affects the choice between competing fault correction histories.
main_problem: The paper investigates the ambiguity arising when different physical fault histories can produce the same detector record but carry opposite logical labels during lattice surgery parity measurements.
main_result: The analysis quantifies the trade-off in decoding performance, showing that while changing single-fault decisions can be beneficial at higher noise, the overall gain is small and the mechanism's predictive power is limited to specific physical channels.
method: The authors use maximum-likelihood methods, full-syndrome probability calculations, and targeted channel attenuation to compare different decoding strategies.
model_or_system: The study models quantum error correction using lattice surgery to perform logical parity measurements, focusing on the competition between single-gate faults and pairs of reset/readout faults.
key_observables: Logical-parity risk $R(D)$, the difference in risk $\Delta$, and the cost/benefit of retaining or modifying single-fault decisions.
important_parameters: Noise strength ($\gamma$), confidence bounds (95%), and specific physical channels implicated in the fault histories.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on comparing specific decoding strategies (e.g., minimum-weight matching vs. fixed modification) and the predictive utility is shown only on a finite grid.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate competing fault histories, joint-probability differences across syndromes at varying noise strengths, and the effect of targeted versus matched channel suppression.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the ambiguity, quantifying the error using full-syndrome probabilities, testing the physical explanation via channel attenuation, and finally assessing the predictive scope of the derived trade-offs.
why_interesting: The detailed analysis of finite-noise decoding trade-offs and the connection to specific physical error channels provides concrete, quantitative insights into the limitations of current fault-tolerance schemes.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Competing fault histories for the complete record S = D63D77, with all other 150 detector bits zero. The upper branch shows one of two single-gate histories carrying L = 0; the lower branch represents four reset/readout pairs carrying L = 1. Each F marker denotes either a Z fault after an X-basis reset or an X-readout flip: on q27 at tick 20 or 25, and on q1 at tick 32 or 37, respectively. The class probabilities favor label zero at γ = 0.10 and label one at γ = 0.50. Changing the decision can reduce average parity error while sacrificing correction of the identified single-gate faults. Circuit excerpts are schematic; the full fault signatures were independently checked.

FIG. 2. Joint-probability differences for the three complete syndromes at two noise strengths. Intervals have simultaneous 95% coverage in the expanded-support experiment, with ten million background samples per scale.

FIG. 4. Override effect for baseline, targeted suppression, and matched suppression. Each condition uses twenty million samples, independent of the noise sweep. The estimates reuse the original control experiment; their displayed intervals use the broader retrospective 27 × 10 family shared with the dense sweeps.

FIG. 3. Paired override effect at seventeen noise scales, with twenty million shots per point. Positive values favor the modification. Intervals use the retrospective simultaneous 95% family of 27 displayed conditions and ten binomial marginals per condition. Six scales reuse the initial sweep; eleven are later additions. Lines connect sampled conditions, not fitted values. The points from γ = 0.175 through 0.30 are unresolved.

FIG. 5. Prediction versus confirmation for the fixed label- one rule in eighteen mixed-bias conditions and three isotropic controls. Color distinguishes the noise composition; circles, squares, and triangles denote γ = 0.10, 0.25, 0.50. Each point uses twenty million fresh shots. Intervals retain the original simultaneous 21 × 14 confirmation family. The dashed line is equality, not a fit. Two exact policy identities coincide at the origin. These points evaluate the fixed rule. Within the eighteen mixed-bias conditions, the prediction-selected policy instead gives six resolved benefits and twelve identities.
